segments: ...spring {OCR?}, and the winter acquired the nature of spring.
And there was joy for the Mongols in the confirmation of their leader,
and for the Christians in the triumph of their confession.
And in this same winter, certain rebel men of the Tatars,
about five thousand,
who had fled and were hiding in the borders of India,
came to the territory of Shiraz,
and wrought great devastation and massive slaughter.
Only into the city were they not able to enter,
but the force that came out and encountered them they crushed,
and only a few barely escaped.
For even the outlaws who were in Shiraz
laid hands on the wealthy,
and plundered their possessions.
Now the son of Malik-Malka,
when he heard of the deeds of those rebels,
pursued them and overtook them,
and put the majority of them to the edge of the sword.
And in the days of spring, there was in Baghdad a certain wicked and insolent executioner in the service of the governor,
and he inflicted evils upon many,
and violated men's wives.
Moreover, he even mocked the great counsellor of the kingdom,
and ridiculed him after the manner of comedy.
And one day, when the governor had gone out hunting,
the counsellor seized that insolent executioner,
fixed a cross for him upon a wagon,
and nailed his hands and his feet.
And he paraded him through the markets of Baghdad,
while two pack-needles were thrust through his tongue.
And a youth stood behind him on the wagon,
and with a fan was brushing the flies away from the wretched man's face.
And he cried out to him, saying:
"Thus are punished those who mock the great!"
And when they brought him out by the Tigris River,
they cut off his head and hung it above the bridge,
and they burned his corpse with fire.
And many evil people were terrified at his destruction.
For it was an amusing sight {OCR?} as they paraded him through the streets,
with a crowd of mimes walking before him, striking cymbals and dancing while mocking him.
And in this same year, on Friday, the nineteenth of Iyyar,
the Egyptian armies assaulted Qal'ah Rumayta (Hromkla):
nine thousand horsemen and four thousand footmen,
with a certain emir named Baysari standing at the head of the Egyptians,
and at the head of the army of Syria, Husam {OCR?} al-Din of Ayn Tab.
